definition: In artificial intelligence, conceptual dependency (or CD) theory is a model of natural language understanding.
details: Roger Schank at Stanford University introduced the model in 1969, in the early days of artificial intelligence. This model was extensively used by Schank's students at Yale University such as Robert Wilensky, Wendy Lehnert, and Janet Kolodner. Schank developed the model to represent knowledge for natural language input into computers. Partly influenced by the work of Sydney Lamb, his goal was to make the meaning independent of the words used in the input, i.e. two sentences identical in meaning would have a single representation. The system was also intended to draw logical inferences. The model uses the following basic representational tokens: real world objects, each with some attributes. real world actions, each with attributes times locations A set of conceptual transitions then act on this representation, e.g. an ATRANS is used to represent a transfer such as "give" or "take" while a PTRANS is used to act on locations such as "move" or "go". An MTRANS represents mental acts such as "tell", etc.
story: Think of a grammar teacher who never memorized a rule but can still tell you when a sentence sounds wrong. The machine learns language the way you did — by hearing so much of it that the patterns sink in. It figures out meaning by noticing which words like to travel together. The machine learns to read between the lines by reading an impossible number of lines. And that is Conceptual dependency — teaching a machine to read between the lines.
